blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a comprehensive measurement study on the decentralization of Bitcoin and Ethereum networks, conducted over 2016-2017. The paper challenges assumptions about decentralization by providing empirical data on mining power distribution, utilization, fairness, and network characteristics. Notably, the study finds that both networks rely heavily on a small number of mining entities, with Bitcoin's top four miners controlling over 53% of power and Ethereum's top three controlling 61%. The paper also reveals that proof-of-work mining is less decentralized than a Byzantine quorum system of size 20, and that miners may obfuscate their true power to appear more decentralized. Other findings include high mining power utilization (99% in Bitcoin, 90-97% in Ethereum) and evidence that top miners in both networks are more successful at appending blocks relative to their mining power, indicating potential centralization pressures.
paper_title: Decentralization in Bitcoin and Ethereum networks
paper_abstract: Blockchain-based cryptocurrencies have demonstrated how to securely implement traditionally centralized systems, such as currencies, in a decentralized fashion. However, there have been few measurement studies on the level of decentralization they achieve in practice. We present a measurement study on various decentralization metrics of two of the leading cryptocurrencies with the largest market capitalization and user base, Bitcoin and Ethereum. We investigate the extent of decentralization by measuring the network resources of nodes and the interconnection among them, the protocol requirements affecting the operation of nodes, and the robustness of the two systems against attacks. In particular, we adapted existing internet measurement techniques and used the Falcon Relay Network as a novel measurement tool to obtain our data. We discovered that neither Bitcoin nor Ethereum has strictly better properties than the other. We also provide concrete suggestions for improving both systems.
